questions.q: A design specification
o: lists the requirements a product must meet
questions.why: It's written after research and used to evaluate.

questions.q: Anthropometrics is
o: the study of human body measurements for design
questions.why: Ergonomics uses this data.

questions.q: What is a design specification?
o: A sketch of the final idea
A list of measurable requirements the product must meet
questions.why: Each point should be testable in evaluation.

questions.q: Which research method gives primary data on how people actually use an existing product?
o: Observing users carrying out the task and recording the problems they meet
Looking up material properties in a data book
questions.why: Primary research is gathered first-hand. Watching real users reveals problems they may not mention. Reviews, data books and patents are secondary sources.

questions.q: What is meant by iterative design?
o: Producing one final drawing and making it
Repeated cycles of prototyping, testing and refining a design
questions.why: Iterative design improves a solution step by step, with each cycle of testing and evaluation informing the next version.

long.q: Write four specification points for a bedside lamp for children aged 5–8. Make each point specific and justify it; generic points such as 'it must be safe' score nothing.
scheme: B1: a specific safety point, justified, e.g. low-voltage LED with no hot surfaces, because children will touch it
B1: a measurable size or stability point, e.g. base at least 120 mm wide so it can't tip over on a bedside table
B1: a user point, e.g. a switch large enough for small hands and reachable from bed
B1: a cost, material or aesthetic point, justified, e.g. a stated maximum price; bright colours that appeal to the age group

long.q: Explain what is meant by an iterative design process, and give two benefits of designing in this way.
scheme: B1: iterative design is a repeated cycle of designing, making a model or prototype, testing and evaluating, then refining
B1: each cycle's test results and user feedback feed into the next version
B1: a benefit, e.g. faults are found early, when they are cheaper to fix
B1: a second benefit, e.g. the final product meets users' needs better because they are involved throughout

long.q: Explain how ergonomics and anthropometric data would influence the design of the handle and controls of a cordless hand drill.
scheme: B1: anthropometric data (hand length, grip diameter) for the intended users is used to size the handle
B1: the grip size is chosen to suit a range such as the 5th to 95th percentile, so most users can hold it securely
B1: the trigger is placed where the index finger naturally rests and needs a comfortable force to operate
B1: the weight, including the battery, is positioned to balance under the hand to reduce wrist strain
B1: a further ergonomic feature, e.g. soft-grip, textured surface to reduce slipping and vibration; controls such as the direction switch reachable with the thumb without changing grip

long.q: Evaluate the use of 3D CAD modelling and rapid prototyping (3D printing) during the development of a new product.
scheme: B1: CAD models can be changed quickly and viewed from any angle, so many variations can be explored
B1: virtual testing (e.g. stress analysis, checking parts fit) reduces the number of physical prototypes
B1: 3D printing makes accurate physical prototypes directly from the CAD file, so form, fit and ergonomics can be checked by users
B1: a limitation, e.g. printed parts may not have the strength or finish of the final material; printers and software are expensive; printing large parts is slow
B1: a justified judgement, e.g. greatly speeds up development and cuts cost, but final tests must still use production materials

long.q: Explain what is meant by 'design for manufacture and assembly', and describe three ways a designer could reduce the cost of assembling a product.
scheme: B1: designing the product from the start so it is easy, quick and cheap to make and put together
B1: a way, e.g. reduce the number of separate parts by combining them into one moulding
B1: a second way, e.g. use snap fits or standard fixings instead of many different screws
B1: a third way, e.g. make parts symmetrical or shaped so they can only fit one way; design for assembly in one direction (from above)

questions.q: Which is a thermoplastic?
questions.why: Thermoplastics can be reheated and reshaped.

questions.q: A hardwood comes from
questions.why: e.g. oak, beech.

questions.q: An alloy is
o: a mixture of a metal with other elements
questions.why: e.g. brass (copper and zinc).

questions.q: Which property describes a material's ability to absorb energy and resist sudden impact without fracturing?
questions.why: Toughness is resistance to fracture under impact. Hardness is resistance to scratching and indentation, and a hard material can still be brittle.

questions.q: Why is a thermosetting plastic such as melamine-formaldehyde used for laminate kitchen worktop surfaces?
o: It can easily be reheated and remoulded
It is hard and heat-resistant, and does not soften when reheated
questions.why: Thermosets form permanent cross-links when cured, so they stay rigid and hard when heated. Remoulding on reheating is a property of thermoplastics.

long.q: Bicycle frames are often made from aluminium alloy rather than mild steel. Give two advantages and one disadvantage of aluminium alloy for this use.
scheme: B1: lower density, so the frame is lighter
B1: resists corrosion (protective oxide layer), so it won't rust
B1: a disadvantage, e.g. more expensive; harder to weld; lower fatigue strength

long.q: Electrical socket covers are often made from urea-formaldehyde. Explain, with reference to its molecular structure, why a thermosetting plastic is suitable for this use.
scheme: B1: thermosetting plastics have strong cross-links between their polymer chains
B1: so they do not soften when heated again; they char instead, which suits parts that may become warm
B1: a good electrical insulator
B1: a further property, e.g. hard and rigid, so it resists knocks and scratches; can be moulded once to a precise shape

long.q: Explain what happens to copper when it is work-hardened, and describe how it can be annealed to restore its properties.
scheme: B1: repeated bending or hammering distorts the grain structure, making the copper harder and more brittle
B1: it then becomes difficult to shape and may crack
B1: annealing: heat the copper to a dull red heat
B1: then cool it (copper can be quenched in water or left to cool), which restores its ductility and softness

long.q: Explain what a composite material is. Give two reasons why carbon-fibre reinforced plastic is used for racing bicycle frames, and one disadvantage.
scheme: B1: a composite combines two or more materials (here carbon fibres in a resin matrix) to give better properties than either alone
B1: a very high strength-to-weight ratio, so the frame is light but strong
B1: a second reason, e.g. very stiff, so pedalling effort isn't lost; fibres can be laid in directions that match the loads; can be moulded into aerodynamic shapes
B1: a disadvantage, e.g. expensive; damage can be hard to see and repair; difficult to recycle

long.q: Explain why timber must be seasoned before use, and compare air seasoning with kiln seasoning.
scheme: B1: freshly felled timber contains a lot of water; seasoning reduces its moisture content
B1: so the timber is more stable (less shrinking, warping or splitting later), stronger and less likely to rot
B1: air seasoning: stacked with spacers under a cover so air circulates; cheap
B1: air seasoning is slow (often about a year per 25 mm thickness) and only reaches the moisture content of the surrounding air
B1: kiln seasoning uses controlled heat and humidity: much faster and can reach a lower moisture content suitable for indoor furniture, but costs more in energy and equipment

questions.q: Injection moulding is best suited to
o: mass production of identical plastic parts
questions.why: High setup cost, very low unit cost.

questions.q: A jig is used to
o: guide a tool so parts are made accurately and repeatably
questions.why: Useful in batch production.

questions.q: Which process makes many identical hollow plastic bottles?
questions.why: Injection moulding makes solid parts; vacuum forming makes thin shells.

questions.q: Which casting process is most suitable for a small, intricate silver jewellery piece?
questions.why: Investment casting reproduces fine detail from a wax pattern and suits small precious-metal parts. Sand casting gives coarse surfaces, die casting needs costly dies for volume, and slip casting is for ceramics.

questions.q: What is the purpose of annealing a metal?
o: To make it as hard as possible by quenching
To coat it with zinc to prevent rust
To give it a decorative chrome finish
To heat it so internal stresses are relieved and it becomes softer and easier to work
questions.why: Work-hardened metal becomes brittle; annealing restores ductility. Hardening, galvanising and plating are different treatments.

long.q: Compare injection moulding and vacuum forming for making 10 000 plastic phone cases.
scheme: B1: injection moulding: high mould cost but very low unit cost at volume
B1: produces precise, detailed, varied wall thickness
B1: vacuum forming: cheap moulds, but thin sheets and less detail
B1: judgement: injection moulding suits 10 000 units

long.q: Toy cars are often made by high-pressure die casting in zinc alloy rather than by sand casting. Explain the differences between the two processes and why die casting suits this product.
scheme: B1: sand casting uses a new sand mould for each casting; die casting forces molten metal into a reusable steel die under pressure
B1: die casting gives a fine surface finish and accurate, thin, detailed parts that need little finishing
B1: dies are expensive, but the unit cost is low at high volume, and cycle times are short
B1: toy cars are made in very large numbers with fine detail, so die casting is the better choice; zinc alloy's low melting point suits it

long.q: Describe how the curved back of a chair could be made by laminating thin wood veneers.
scheme: B1: a former (mould) is made to the required curve, often a matching male and female pair
B1: thin veneers are cut to size, with the grain usually running along the length
B1: glue (e.g. urea-formaldehyde or PVA) is spread on each veneer and they are stacked
B1: the stack is pressed against the former with clamps or a vacuum bag and left until the glue cures
B1: the lamination is removed (it keeps the curve with little spring-back) and the edges are trimmed and finished

long.q: Give two advantages and one disadvantage of using CNC machining instead of manual machining for batch production of aluminium parts.
scheme: B1: every part is identical and accurate to tight tolerances
B1: a second advantage, e.g. faster; can run unattended for long periods; complex shapes are possible; fewer skilled operators needed
B1: a disadvantage, e.g. high cost of machines; time to program and set up; less economic for a single item

long.q: A shaft is specified as 25.00 ± 0.05 mm in diameter. (a) State the upper and lower limits. (b) Three shafts measure 24.93 mm, 25.04 mm and 25.06 mm. State which would be accepted. (c) Explain why manufacturers specify tolerances.
scheme: B1: (a) upper limit 25.05 mm, lower limit 24.95 mm
B1: (b) only the 25.04 mm shaft is accepted
B1: (b) 24.93 mm is below the lower limit and 25.06 mm is above the upper limit, so both are rejected
B1: (c) no process is perfectly accurate; tolerances set how much variation still lets parts fit and work, so parts are interchangeable

questions.q: Designing for disassembly helps
o: recycling and repair at the end of a product's life
questions.why: Part of the circular economy.

questions.q: What does a life cycle assessment consider?
o: The environmental impact from raw materials to disposal
questions.why: Includes manufacture, transport, use and end of life.

questions.q: Which design choice makes a product easier to recycle?
o: Using a single material that is easy to separate
questions.why: Design for disassembly helps reuse and recycling.

questions.q: Which is an example of a closed-loop (circular economy) approach?
o: Sending products to landfill at the end of their life
A manufacturer takes back used products and recovers materials to make new ones
Burning products without recovering any energy
questions.why: In a closed loop, materials are kept in use by recovery and remanufacture instead of being discarded after one life.

questions.q: Why can a product with high embodied energy still be the more sustainable choice?
o: Because embodied energy does not affect sustainability
Because higher energy always means higher quality
Because it lasts much longer and replaces many short-lived alternatives over its life
Because it costs more to buy
questions.why: Life cycle assessment looks at the whole life: a durable product can have a lower total impact per year of use than several disposable ones.

long.q: Describe the stages of a life cycle assessment for a reusable stainless steel water bottle, and give one environmental impact at three different stages.
scheme: B1: stages named in order: raw materials, manufacture, distribution, use, end of life
B1: raw materials: mining iron ore, chromium and nickel uses energy and damages habitats
B1: manufacture: smelting and forming steel uses a lot of energy, giving CO₂ emissions
B1: another stage, e.g. use: washing uses water and energy; end of life: steel can be recycled repeatedly

long.q: Explain what is meant by a circular economy, and describe how it could be applied to the design of office chairs.
scheme: B1: a circular economy keeps products and materials in use for as long as possible instead of 'make, use, dispose'
B1: application, e.g. chairs designed to be repaired, with replaceable seat pads, castors and gas lifts
B1: application, e.g. parts made from single, labelled materials and fixed with screws so they can be separated for recycling
B1: application, e.g. a take-back or leasing scheme so the manufacturer refurbishes and resells used chairs

long.q: Analyse the design of an aluminium drinks can. Explain why aluminium is used, how the can body is made, and how its design supports recycling.
scheme: B1: aluminium is lightweight, so transport energy is low
B1: it does not rust and is a good barrier to light and air, protecting the drink
B1: the body is made from one piece by pressing a disc into a cup, then drawing and ironing the walls very thin (deep drawing)
B1: the domed base and the pressure of the drink make the thin walls strong enough to stack
B1: it is almost entirely one material, so it is easy to sort (with eddy current separators) and can be recycled repeatedly using far less energy than making new aluminium

long.q: Explain why national and international standards (for example from ISO or BSI) are important to manufacturers and to consumers.
scheme: B1: manufacturers: products and parts that meet a standard are compatible and interchangeable (e.g. thread sizes, paper sizes)
B1: manufacturers: meeting standards allows products to be sold in many countries and reduces legal risk
B1: consumers: standards set minimum levels of safety and quality
B1: consumers: a recognised mark gives confidence that a product has been tested

long.q: Explain three ways a designer could reduce the environmental impact of distributing a large item of furniture to customers.
scheme: B1: flat-pack design so more items fit in each lorry or container
B1: lighter components or materials, reducing fuel used in transport
B1: reduced or recyclable packaging, e.g. card corners instead of expanded polystyrene
B1: a link explained to lower fuel use and emissions per item (or making locally to shorten journeys)

questions.q: An exploded drawing shows
questions.why: Parts are drawn spaced along their assembly lines.

questions.q: Orthographic projection shows
o: front, side and plan views to scale
questions.why: Used for manufacturing drawings.

questions.q: What does third-angle orthographic projection show?
o: Front, plan and side views laid out with standard positions
questions.why: The plan goes above the front view in third angle.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of a 3D CAD model over hand sketches at the development stage?
o: It can be rotated, modified and tested virtually, then exported for CAM or rendering
It needs no skill to produce
It is always faster for first ideas
It removes the need for a specification
questions.why: CAD models can be edited, analysed and sent straight to manufacture. Hand sketching is usually quicker for generating first ideas.

questions.q: A sectional view on an engineering drawing is used to
o: show the colour and texture of materials
show internal details by imagining the object cut through, with cut surfaces hatched
questions.why: Sections reveal hidden internal features clearly, with hatching on the cut faces, instead of relying on confusing hidden-detail lines.

long.q: In third-angle orthographic projection, where is the plan drawn, and where is the view from the right-hand side drawn? Sketch the layout of the three views and add the third-angle projection symbol.
scheme: B1: plan drawn directly above the front elevation
B1: view from the right drawn to the right of the front elevation
B1: correct symbol: the cone's side view on the left, its two circles on the right

long.q: Explain the purpose of an exploded view, and give two drawing conventions used in exploded views.
scheme: B1: it shows how the parts of a product fit together and the order of assembly
B1: a convention, e.g. parts are moved apart along the lines (axes) they assemble along
B1: a second convention, e.g. thin chain or dashed lines show how parts line up; parts are often numbered and listed in a parts list

long.q: Describe how a sectional view is shown on an orthographic drawing.
scheme: B1: a cutting plane is shown on another view by a chain line, thickened at the ends and at changes of direction
B1: arrows on the cutting plane show the viewing direction, and it is labelled (e.g. A–A) to match the section title
B1: cut surfaces are hatched with thin lines, usually at 45°
B1: adjacent parts are hatched in opposite directions or at different spacing; solid shafts, bolts and webs cut along their length are not hatched

long.q: Explain two advantages and one disadvantage of using CAD rendering rather than hand rendering when presenting design proposals to a client.
scheme: B1: photorealistic images show real materials, colours and lighting, so the client can visualise the finished product
B1: a second advantage, e.g. colours or materials can be changed instantly to show options; the model can be rotated or animated
B1: a disadvantage, e.g. takes time and skill to set up; costly software; a polished render can look final, discouraging changes at an early stage

long.q: (a) A component 360 mm long is drawn to a scale of 1:4. Calculate its length on the drawing. (b) A small detail 6 mm long is drawn to a scale of 5:1. Calculate its drawn length. (c) Explain why a detail might be drawn at an enlarged scale.
scheme: B1: (c) small features would be too small to see and dimension clearly at full size

questions.q: A potential divider with an LDR can be used to
o: switch on a light when it gets dark
questions.why: The LDR's resistance rises in the dark.

questions.q: A cam converts
questions.why: The follower rises and falls.

questions.q: In a control system, what is an input transducer?
o: A sensor that turns a physical change into an electrical signal
questions.why: For example a thermistor or light-dependent resistor.

questions.q: A potential divider has R1 = 10 kΩ at the top and R2 = 10 kΩ at the bottom, with a 6 V supply. What is the output voltage across R2?
questions.why: Vout = Vin × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2) = 6 × 10 ÷ 20 = 3 V. With equal resistors, the supply is shared equally.

questions.q: In a control circuit, a transistor is often used to
o: act as a switch, letting a small input current control a larger current to an output device
store electrical charge for later use
questions.why: A sensor circuit gives only a small current; the transistor switches enough current to drive a motor, lamp or buzzer. Storing charge is a capacitor's job.

long.q: A driver gear with 20 teeth meshes with a driven gear with 60 teeth. The driver turns at 300 rpm. Calculate the gear ratio and the output speed, and state the direction the driven gear turns.
scheme: M1: gear ratio = driven ÷ driver = 60 ÷ 20 = 3 : 1
A1: output speed = 300 ÷ 3 = 100 rpm
B1: the driven gear turns in the opposite direction

long.q: In a compound gear train, gear A (15 teeth) drives gear B (45 teeth). Gear C (20 teeth) is fixed on the same shaft as B and drives gear D (60 teeth). Gear A turns clockwise at 900 rpm. (a) Calculate the overall velocity ratio. (b) Calculate the output speed of gear D. (c) State the direction gear D turns.
scheme: B1: (c) clockwise (B and C turn anticlockwise; D reverses again)

long.q: Describe how a single-acting pneumatic cylinder is controlled by a push-button-operated 3/2 valve, from pressing the button to releasing it.
scheme: B1: pressing the button switches the 3/2 valve so compressed air flows from the supply port to the cylinder
B1: air pressure pushes the piston and the piston rod moves out (outstrokes)
B1: releasing the button lets the spring return the valve, which connects the cylinder to the exhaust port
B1: the air escapes and the cylinder's internal spring pushes the piston back in (instrokes)

long.q: A security light should come on when it is dark (D = 1) AND movement is detected (M = 1), OR when a manual override switch is on (S = 1). (a) Write a Boolean expression for the output Q. (b) State the output Q for: (i) D = 1, M = 0, S = 0; (ii) D = 1, M = 1, S = 0; (iii) D = 0, M = 0, S = 1.
scheme: B1: (a) Q = (D AND M) OR S (accept Q = D·M + S)
B1: (b)(iii) Q = 1

long.q: A steel tie rod in a frame structure has a cross-sectional area of 50 mm² and carries a tensile load of 10 kN. (a) Calculate the tensile stress in the rod in N/mm². (b) The yield stress of the steel is 250 N/mm². Calculate the factor of safety against yielding.
scheme: M1: (a) stress = force ÷ area = 10 000 N ÷ 50 mm²
A1: (a) 200 N/mm² (200 MPa)
M1: (b) factor of safety = yield stress ÷ working stress = 250 ÷ 200

questions.q: A design brief
o: is a short statement of the problem to be solved
questions.why: The specification comes after research.

questions.q: What should the evaluation of a design project do?
o: Test the product against the specification and suggest justified improvements
questions.why: Use evidence from tests and users.

questions.q: Why build and test models during development?
o: To check function, size and appearance before the final product
questions.why: Record what each model taught you.

questions.q: Which is the best way to generate a range of initial ideas?
o: Quickly sketch and annotate several different solutions before choosing one to develop
Draw one detailed idea in full colour
Copy the first product found online
questions.why: A range of annotated ideas shows creative thinking and lets the designer compare options against the specification before committing.

questions.q: Why should a folio record changes made during manufacture?
o: Because the product must exactly match the first idea
To hide mistakes from the examiner
To show problem-solving and explain why the final product differs from the plan
questions.why: Documented modifications show the designer responding to problems during making, which is evidence of real decision-making.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of CAD/CAM?
o: accurate, repeatable manufacture from digital designs
questions.why: Accuracy, speed and repeatability.

questions.q: What is meant by ergonomics?
o: Designing products to fit the people who use them
questions.why: Uses anthropometric data, such as hand sizes.

questions.q: What is planned obsolescence?
o: Making a product last for ever
Designing a product to have a limited useful life
questions.why: It raises sustainability concerns.

questions.q: Which is an example of inclusive design?
o: A luxury kettle made in a limited edition
A kettle designed for one celebrity client
A kettle with a large, easy-grip handle and a clear water gauge so that users with limited grip or sight can use it
A kettle with very small buttons to look sleek
questions.why: Inclusive design aims to make products usable by as wide a range of people as possible, including older and disabled users, without needing a special version.

questions.q: What does just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing aim to do?
o: Deliver materials and components only as they are needed, reducing the stock held
Store large stocks in case of shortages
Send all products by air freight
questions.why: JIT cuts storage costs and waste by matching supply closely to production, but it depends on reliable suppliers.

long.q: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of planned obsolescence for manufacturers, consumers and the environment. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: manufacturers: repeat sales and steadier income
B1: consumers: regular improvements and often lower initial prices
B1: consumers: replacing products sooner costs more; parts often can't be repaired
B1: environment: more waste (especially e-waste) and more resources and energy used
B1: a justified conclusion, e.g. referring to right-to-repair rules or designing for longevity

long.q: Explain how patents, registered designs and copyright each protect a designer's work.
scheme: B1: a patent protects a new invention (how it works or is made), giving the holder sole rights for a limited time, usually up to 20 years
B1: a patent must be applied for, and the invention disclosed publicly in return
B1: a registered design protects the appearance of a product (shape, pattern, decoration), not how it works
B1: copyright protects original drawings, written work and software automatically, without registration

long.q: Discuss the influence of the Bauhaus on the design of products today. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: the Bauhaus (Germany, 1919–1933) linked art, craft and industry
B1: its products used simple geometric forms with no unnecessary decoration, with form following function
B1: it designed for mass production using modern materials, e.g. Marcel Breuer's tubular steel chairs
B1: a specific modern example of the influence, e.g. minimalist consumer electronics; flat-pack furniture; clean sans-serif typography
B1: a reasoned conclusion, e.g. much modern 'minimalist' design follows Bauhaus principles, though today's designers also value personalisation and ornament

long.q: Explain what is meant by inclusive design, and describe how a kitchen vegetable peeler could be designed for users with arthritis in their hands.
scheme: B1: inclusive design creates products that can be used by as many people as possible, including older or disabled users, without special adaptation
B1: a thick, soft, non-slip handle so it can be gripped with little force
B1: a further feature, e.g. a wide-angle or swivelling blade so the wrist doesn't need to twist; a lightweight design
B1: testing with users who have arthritis to check comfort and grip

long.q: Evaluate how a manufacturer could use the product life cycle and market research to decide when to launch a redesigned version of a product. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: the stages named: introduction, growth, maturity, decline
B1: sales level off in maturity and fall in decline, so a redesign is often planned in late maturity to extend the life cycle
B1: market research (sales data, surveys, focus groups) shows what users want changed and what competitors offer
B1: a limitation, e.g. the stages are only clear in hindsight; research can be costly and users may not know what they want
B1: a supported judgement, e.g. using both together lowers the risk of launching too early (wasting the current product's sales) or too late (losing customers)

topics.name: A Level design and make project

questions.q: An A Level project evaluation should
o: test the product against the specification, with users
questions.why: Objective testing and user feedback.

questions.q: Why is a Gantt chart useful in a project?
o: It plans tasks against time so progress can be checked
questions.why: Update it as the project changes.

questions.q: What makes a client's feedback useful?
o: It is recorded and used to change the design
It is collected after the exam
questions.why: Show how each change came from evidence.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of interviewing the client at the start of an A Level project?
o: To ask them to design the product
To establish their needs, constraints and preferences, which shape the brief and specification
To agree the final colour only
To get their approval of the finished product
questions.why: Early client input defines the real problem, so the brief and specification are grounded in the user's needs rather than the designer's assumptions.

questions.q: Why should an A Level project include a risk assessment for the making stage?
o: To identify hazards and control measures so the product can be made safely
questions.why: A risk assessment identifies each hazard in the processes used and how it will be controlled, which is part of planning safe manufacture.
